task.title: Run the board behind a sign-in proxy
task.description:
Workbook reaches only people who can push to the repository. A client PM who should read and edit stories but never touch the code has no way in. The answer is not a hosted product: Workbook is open source with a CLI and a web API, and anyone can build their own tool, permissions and screens on those. This story is the small amount of work that lets someone put the existing board on a server, behind whatever sign-in they already use.

Workbook itself gains no sign-in, no accounts, no invites and no roles. A sign-in proxy in front of the board decides who gets in and tells the board who each person is.

An earlier version of this story described a companion app with its own accounts and invites. That design was dropped as too opinionated; its text is in this task's history.

## What is needed

- **The board has to accept its public address.** It answers only requests addressed to the exact local address it is bound to, over plain HTTP. On 0.6.0, requests shaped the way a proxy would send them for `https://tasks.example.com` were refused, both a read and an edit. The person deploying it needs a way to tell `workbook serve` the address people will actually open, and the protections against other websites driving the board have to hold for that address.
- **The board has to take each person's name from the proxy.** The proxy signs the person in and passes their name in a request header, which is how such proxies normally work. The board records that person's edits under that name, building on "Record an edit under a name other than the checkout's Git email".
- **That header is off unless turned on.** A board that believes a name from any request lets anyone who can reach its port be anyone. Honoring it is a deliberate choice by whoever deploys it, and the guide says plainly that the board must then be reachable only through the proxy.
- **Who is looking matters for reads too.** The board shows which assignments are yours and which you may remove. Today that is one answer for the whole server, and it has to become one answer per person.
- **A hosting guide with one worked example.** It starts from a tasks-only folder, covers the credential the server holds, puts one named sign-in proxy in front, and ends with a board on an https address.

## What the guide has to be honest about

- **The server's key opens the whole repository.** The first version is tested with a deploy key on the code repository, so a break-in can read the code even though none of it is on the server's disk. A second, tasks-only repository removes that. It is the follow-up "Support multiple task remotes", which now comes after this story.
- **A contributor is one person in two places.** The name the proxy passes has to match the `user.email` in their checkout, or Workbook treats them as two people.
- **A save and its publication are a moment apart.** On a host that wipes its disk on restart, an edit saved but not yet published is lost. The guide says what to use to avoid that.
- **The board has only ever had one trusted user.** Before this is recommended to anyone, review what changes when several people use one board: how one person's task text and attachments are shown in another person's browser, and request and upload limits.

## Decisions to settle before building

Settle these first and record the outcome on this task; each one that turns into real work becomes its own task depending on this one.

1. How the public address and the name header are configured.
2. What happens to a request with no name when the header is turned on. Proposed: refuse it, so a misconfigured proxy cannot record everyone's edits under the server's own name.
3. Whether the board relies only on being unreachable except through the proxy, or also checks a secret the proxy sends.
4. Which sign-in proxy and which host the worked example uses.
5. Decided 2026-11-18: the guide recommends a deploy key with write access as the server's credential. It is tied to one repository, stays under the repository owner's control, and needs nothing to renew it. Who may sign in is decided separately, at the proxy. Confirm the deploy key details against GitHub's documentation when writing the guide.

## Done when

- Following only the guide, a person runs the board at an https address behind a sign-in proxy they chose. Nobody on the Workbook project registers or runs anything for them.
- Two people signed in through the proxy each make an edit, and a contributor's `workbook show --history` in a code checkout shows each edit under that person's own name.
- Each of them sees their own assignments as theirs on the board, and can remove only what Workbook lets that name remove.
- With the header left off, a request that carries it is treated like any other and the name in it is ignored.
- A request from another website is still refused at the public address.
- An edit made on the hosted board and a different edit to the same field made from the CLI at the same time both survive as a visible conflict.
- `workbook serve` with no new options behaves exactly as it does today.
- The README links the guide, `docs/reference.md` documents the options, and `docs/architecture.md` says a name passed by a proxy is asserted like any other.
